prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Pirates captured a Belgian ship and said they were taking it to the coast of Somalia after the vessel was reported missing early Saturday, NATO and pirate sources told CNN. The Dutch frigate De Zeven Provincien tracked seven pirates Saturday back to their mother ship. The Pompei, a Belgian-registered ship believed to have a mostly Belgian and Croatian crew, was one of two vessels that came under attack near the Indian Ocean island nation of Seychelles on Saturday, the sources said. The second ship escaped the attack after a brief exchange of gunfire with pirate vessels, the pirate source added. Meanwhile, Dutch naval forces captured seven pirates and freed 20 captive fishermen after tracking the pirates to their "mother ship" in the western Gulf of Aden on Saturday, a NATO maritime spokesman said. The Belgian government tried to communicate with the Pompei "without success" before the ship was confirmed to have been hijacked, according to an official.  See an interactive map of 2009 pirate attacks off the Horn of Africa » . "This morning we received two different channels, a silent alert, that there was a problem on the boat, which is a Belgian boat on its way to Seychelles," Belgium Government Crisis Center spokesman Peter Martens told reporters. "We tried to have a contact with the ship but without success until now." The archipelago where the attack occurred is roughly 800 miles off the Somali coastline. "Somali pirates are getting wilder and out of control," pirate spokesman Ali Sugulle said on April 11. "They go too far away from the Somali [coast] and go to the Kenyan coast even." The European Union, NATO and the United States have been patrolling the waters off Somalia since an upsurge in piracy in the region last year. No NATO vessels were in the region at the time of the attack, said Cmdr. Chris Davies from NATO's Maritime Component Command Headquarters in Northwood, England. Meanwhile, the Dutch rescue operation happened after pirates launched an unsuccessful attack on petroleum tanker MT Handytankers Magic, NATO Cmdr. Chris Davies told CNN. The Dutch frigate De Zeven Provincien was with the NATO fleet patrolling the region. After the Dutch disarmed the pirates, they released them, Shona Lowe, a spokeswoman from the maritime headquarters, told CNN. Because the crew was on a NATO mission, they lacked the jurisdiction to hold them, according to reports. The MT Handytankers Magic is part of a fleet belonging to Handytankers, a company that distributes petroleum products in Europe, the Mediterranean, and the United States, according to the company's Web site. Last week pirates attacked a U.S.-flagged ship, the Maersk Alabama, off the Somali coast.  The crew regained control of the ship but the captain was taken hostage and held for five days on a lifeboat.  The crisis ended when U.S. Navy sharpshooters shot and killed three of the pirates who were holding the captain. Journalist Mohammed Amiin contributed to this report.

**BRUSSELS, Belgium —** Somali pirates hijacked a Belgian-flagged vessel in the Indian Ocean near the Seychelles, officials said, in the latest attack underscoring the expanding reach of piracy far beyond Somalia’s coastline.

The vessel, the **Pompei**, was seized Saturday while operating in waters northeast of the Seychelles, Belgian officials said. The ship, a dredging vessel owned by a Belgian company, had a multinational crew aboard.

Belgian authorities said they were working with international partners to monitor the situation and safeguard the crew.

“Our priority is the safety of the crew,” a Belgian government official said, adding that authorities were in contact with the ship’s owner and foreign partners. Officials declined to discuss any possible negotiations, citing security concerns.

NATO said naval forces in the region were alerted after the ship sent a distress signal. The alliance has been conducting counter-piracy patrols off the Horn of Africa and in the wider Indian Ocean as Somali pirate groups have moved farther from shore in search of commercial vessels.

A NATO official said allied ships were “responding within the limits of their mandate” and coordinating with other naval forces operating in the region.

The Dutch Defense Ministry also confirmed that a Dutch naval vessel participating in NATO’s anti-piracy mission had been directed toward the area. Dutch officials said the response was part of ongoing efforts to deter pirate activity and protect commercial shipping lanes.

A Dutch defense spokesman said naval forces were “closely following developments” but warned that military action is complicated once pirates have control of a vessel and crew members are held hostage.

The hijacking of the Pompei comes amid a surge in Somali pirate attacks in 2009. Pirates operating from Somalia’s lawless coastline have increasingly used so-called “mother ships” to launch attacks hundreds of miles offshore, reaching waters near the Seychelles and deep into the Indian Ocean.

The waters off Somalia and the Gulf of Aden are among the world’s busiest shipping routes, linking Europe, Asia and the Middle East. International navies, including NATO, the European Union and a U.S.-led maritime task force, have deployed warships to the region, but officials have repeatedly said the area is too vast to patrol completely.

In recent months, Somali pirates have seized cargo ships, tankers and fishing vessels, often holding crews for ransom. The attacks have raised insurance costs, forced some shipping companies to reroute vessels around southern Africa, and increased pressure on governments to respond more aggressively.

The hijacking near the Seychelles follows several high-profile incidents, including the seizure of large commercial vessels and attacks on ships carrying humanitarian aid. International concern intensified after pirates targeted ships far from the Somali coast, demonstrating greater range and coordination.

Maritime analysts say pirates often avoid direct confrontation with warships once hostages are aboard, betting that navies will not risk an assault that could endanger crew members.

“The challenge is not simply finding the pirates,” one maritime security analyst said. “It is what you do after a ship has been taken. Once hostages are involved, the options narrow very quickly.”

Belgian officials said they would continue working through diplomatic and military channels. The ship’s owner was also expected to coordinate with authorities and families of crew members.

No injuries were immediately reported, and officials did not release details on the pirates’ demands.
